subject: Agriculture
title: The EAT-Lancet Diet
description: A micro-lesson that makes The EAT-Lancet Diet usable.

hook.text: In 2019, 37 scientists designed a diet that could feed 10 billion people without destroying the planet.

buildup.text: The EAT-Lancet 'planetary health diet' centers on vegetables, fruits, nuts, legumes, and whole grains.

discovery.text: It allows 14 grams of red meat per day—about one small burger per week. Dairy and eggs are limited too.

twist.text: For Americans, it means 80% less beef. For Indians, it means more animal protein. One diet, different transitions.

climax.text: If adopted globally, the diet could prevent 11 million premature deaths per year while staying within planetary boundaries.

punchline.text: One diet to feed humanity and save the planet. The menu is ready—acceptance isn't.

quiz.question: How much red meat does the EAT-Lancet planetary health diet recommend daily?

details.summary: The EAT-Lancet diet is a science-based reference diet designed to be both nutritionally optimal for humans and sustainable for the planet. This topic covers its recommended food groups, limits on animal products, and the debate over its feasibility and cultural relevance.
details.whyItMatters: The EAT-Lancet Commission showed that feeding 10 billion people a healthy diet within planetary boundaries is possible but requires dramatic shifts in what the world eats and produces.
takeaways: The diet recommends halving global meat and sugar consumption by 2050
Fruits, vegetables, nuts, legumes, and whole grains form the foundation of the diet
Critics argue the diet is too restrictive and culturally insensitive for many populations

faq.question: What does the EAT-Lancet diet recommend?
faq.answer: The diet centers on whole grains, legumes, fruits, vegetables, and nuts, with small amounts of fish, poultry, and dairy. It limits red meat to about 14 grams per day and sugar to 31 grams, roughly halving current global averages.

faq.question: Is the EAT-Lancet diet realistic for everyone?
faq.answer: Critics note it may be unaffordable for the poorest populations, culturally inappropriate for pastoralist and indigenous communities, and difficult to implement without massive food system changes. It works best as a directional guideline, not a rigid prescription.
